ns_taverna.text: Meze tonight? Don't order anything else. We bring you dips, then salad, then halloumi, then sheftalia, then lamb, then you beg us to stop, then the fruit.
Kopiaste! That's Cypriot: 'come and join us'. You say it to anyone passing while you're eating. And then they sit down. That's the risk.

ns_teacher_el.text: Yiá sou! Hello, to one person; 'yiá sas' to more than one, or to be polite. 'Kaliméra' is good morning, 'efcharistó' is thank you.
'Parakaló' is please, and also 'you're welcome', and also what the shopkeeper says when you walk in. One word, three jobs. Very efficient people, the Greeks.
Cypriot Greek has its own sound: Cypriots often say 'éla', come on, and they tend to soften a 'k' into a 'ch' sound. Mainland Greeks can tell a Cypriot in one word.

then.text: Look after that agrino. The real ones are still up in the Paphos forest, wild and wary, and counting on all of us.
You found a Chamelet? People walk past those for years without seeing one. You've got the patience for the hills.
Then take this one. A young agrino, the mouflon of Cyprus, raised at a forest station and too used to people to go back up the mountain. It needs someone who'll walk it.

else.text: Catch a Chamelet. They're in the fields round Pyla and the dunes over in Spain, if you ever go. Look twice at every leaf.
I'm with the Forestry Department, down from the Paphos forest for a meeting and a decent lunch.

Up there we look after the agrino, the Cypriot mouflon, a wild sheep found nowhere else. It was hunted almost to nothing a hundred years ago. Protected since, it's come back to the thousands. It's on your one, two and five cent coins.
I've a young one that needs a keeper. But you'd need a good eye. Show me you can find a Chamelet, the shyest creature on this island, and we'll talk.
